symbolGuide:
| Symbol | Name | Meaning | Turn it up |
| S | Software | The stock of methods. S = 2 means today's methods get as much from compute as twice the compute did before. | |
| C | Training compute | The computing power used to train models. | |
| C_r | Training compute ratio | Training compute showing in models, against baseline | |
| L | Research labour | People plus their AI help, in researcher-equivalents, compared with baseline. 2 means twice the baseline. | More methods, at a falling rate. |
| E | Experiment compute | Computing power for research experiments, compared with baseline. | More methods, at a falling rate. |
| A | Research productivity | How much the lab finds from a given effort, compared with baseline. Below 1 means ideas have got harder to find. | Less labour needed. |
| g | Software growth | How fast S grows, in doublings a year. | |
| g₀ | Baseline software growth | How fast S grew before the speedup. | |
| c | Training growth | How fast training compute grows, in doublings a year. | |
| c₀ | Baseline training growth | How fast training compute grew before the speedup. | |
| G | Software speedup | The new pace of software divided by the old pace. | |
| F | Research production function | Turns labour and experiment compute into research output. F = 1 at baseline. | |
| T_g | Required research output | The value of F the lab must reach to hit the target. | |
| a | Labour weight | How much labour counts in research, against experiment compute. | Labour matters more, so less of it is needed. |
| σ | Elasticity of substitution | How easily people can stand in for compute. 1 is Cobb-Douglas. | People and compute swap more easily. |
| ρ | Substitution parameter | σ rewritten for the CES formula: ρ = (σ − 1)/σ. | |
| λ | Returns to scale | What happens to research output when both inputs grow together. 1 means it grows in step. Below 1 means researchers start to duplicate each other. | Each input goes further. |
| β | Ideas getting harder | Each extra doubling of S multiplies A by 2^−β. 0 means ideas do not get harder. | Labour needed climbs faster over time. |
| K, k | Total compute | The whole compute pool. k compares it with the baseline path. | More for both experiments and training. |
| φ₀, φ₁ | Experiment share | The share of compute that goes to experiments, before and after. | More for experiments, less for training. |
| W | Compute-change period | The years over which a change in training compute takes effect. | The same change adds less to yearly growth. |
| T₀ | Baseline pace | Growth of effective compute before the speedup, in doublings a year. Illustrative. | |
| s | Software share | The part of baseline progress that came from software. Tejas supposes two-thirds. | |
| X | Target speedup | The reported speedup the model tries to reach. METR's estimate is about 2. | More labour needed. |
| X_e | Effective compute speedup | The speedup in effective compute, after h and b. | |
| X_out | Index speedup | The reported index speedup implied by the inputs, given b and h | |
| h | AI share | The assumed share of the acceleration that AI caused. It gives a labour equivalent for that part, and does not identify the actual uplift. | |
| b | Index bridge | An assumed link between the index speedup and the effective compute speedup. We have no estimate of it. | |
| D(t) | Extra software doublings | How many more doublings S has had by year t than on the baseline path. It is negative if S has fallen behind. | |
| A(t) | Productivity at year t | A after t years at the fast pace. | |
| L₀, K₀ | Baseline levels | Starting amounts of labour and compute, for display. They cancel out, so they do not change any result. | |

modelIntroduction:
"If AI has doubled Anthropic's pace, Tejas's model says that's like having about 6 times the research workforce.
On the same model, doubling the pace again would take about 30 times the original workforce." "Based on [a short model](post link) by Tejas Subramaniam, using METR's estimate that Anthropic's models are improving about twice as fast as before on well-specified tasks." "Where this comes from" "What the number depends on" "Tejas called his post a scrappy summary, his loose impression of tweets by Ryan Greenblatt, Ajeya Cotra and others. He says falling research productivity could push the figure much higher. This page builds his model so you can change its assumptions. The starting software share, Cobb-Douglas form, labour weight, A and E are his, and the 2x is METR's. The compute split, the time path and the other settings are ours."
scenarioDescriptions:
| Name | Gloss |
| Tejas's model | His assumptions, unchanged. |
| Research productivity falls 20% | The same effort finds 20% less. |
| Twice the experiment compute | Training compute stays on its old path. |
| Twice the compute everywhere | Experiments and training both double. Depends on our illustrative T₀ and W. METR is confident the acceleration was not due to faster training compute scaling. |
| AI caused 80% of the speedup | METR's guess. This is the labour equivalent of AI's part only, and it depends on where the other causes act. |
| People can't fully replace compute | Researchers share experiment compute, so extra people help less (σ = 0.75). |
| People can barely replace compute | Past a point, more people add almost nothing, and compute sets a limit (σ = 0.5). |

researchEquations:
"This equation makes new methods. Its output is a pace: how fast S grows. Its inputs are people and experiment compute. With equal weights and λ = 1, neither input can do the work alone: four times the people only doubles the pace. A scales the whole result. If ideas get harder to find, A falls and the same lab finds less. Cobb-Douglas builds in one fixed answer to how easily people can stand in for compute, so no symbol for it appears here. Choose CES below to set it yourself."
"within 0.000001"
"F combines L and E; a weights labour and 1 − a weights experiments."
"This equation makes new methods. Its output is a pace: how fast S grows. Its inputs are people and experiment compute. A scales the whole result. If ideas get harder to find, A falls and the same lab finds less. σ says how easily people can stand in for compute. ρ is the same number rewritten for the formula. Below σ = 1 they are hard to swap, and past some point more people add little. Above 1, either input can do it alone."
"within 0.000001"
"Read the shape of the line. Its size depends on β and on g₀, which comes from T₀. Both are our illustrative numbers."
researchLabour:
"Better methods come from a research lab. The lab needs researchers, human or AI, and computing power for experiments, and he weights them equally. Add researchers without adding experiment compute and each extra one adds less. That is why 2.5 times the pace of new methods takes 2.5 × 2.5 = 6.25 times the labour."
"Research labour here means human researchers plus AI doing research work, measured in researcher-equivalents. A 6.25 is the total, including the original 1, and it does not mean 6.25 times the staff. AI raises effective research labour when it adds research capacity or lets the existing team do more. Replacing a human researcher with equal AI capacity leaves this measure unchanged. Adding research labour adds no experiment compute."
"Human researchers plus AI doing research work, in researcher-equivalents, compared with baseline. 2 means twice the baseline."
"How far more research labour can stand in for more experiments. 1 is Cobb-Douglas."
"Labour and experiments swap more easily."
"Thinking can't fully replace experiments"
"Researchers, human or AI, share experiment compute, so extra labour helps less (σ = 0.75)."
"Thinking can barely replace experiments"
"Past a point, more researchers, human or AI, add almost nothing, and experiment compute sets a limit (σ = 0.5)."
"With a = 0.5 and λ = 1, this is Tejas's equation: G = A × √L × √E."
"Only b × h enters. Lowering h means more of the reported speedup comes from outside AI, so the same inputs report a larger speedup. With h below 1, the labour figure covers only the part attributed to AI. The target X enters through X_e = 1 + b × h × (X − 1)."
